adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/protocol/oidc/encode/DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.java:74 — A custom grant returning the documented three-character shortcut produces token IDs that this decoder always rejects because the writer concatenates the unrestricted shortcut while the reader requires exactly six context characters and reads only two grant characters (confidence 100; severity P2; blocking; code: `if (encodedContext.length() != 6) {`).

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that a 3-character shortcut would cause issues, but examining the diff shows all grant shortcuts are exactly 2 characters (e.g., 'ac', 'cc', 'rt', 'pg', 'pc', 'ro', 'te', 'ci', 'dg'). The encoder concatenates sessionType shortcut (2 chars) + tokenType shortcut (2 chars) + grantType shortcut (2 chars) = 6 chars total, which matches the decoder's expectation of exactly 6 characters. The Javadoc comment says 'usually like 3-letters shortcut' but this is just documentation guidance, and all actual implementations use 2-character shortcuts. The code is consistent.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/protocol/oidc/encode/DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.java:113 — Deploying a new grant whose shortcut duplicates an existing grant bypasses the startup uniqueness check and overwrites the reverse mapping, so decoding already-issued tokens reports the new grant while both grants continue issuing the same discriminator (confidence 100; severity P2; blocking; code: `grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantType);`).

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a race condition issue. In getShortcutByGrantType() and getGrantTypeByShortcut(), when a new grant type is deployed at runtime, the code updates the maps without any synchronization or validation that the shortcut is unique. The startup check in postInit() validates uniqueness by comparing map sizes, but runtime additions via these methods bypass this check. If a newly deployed grant has a duplicate shortcut, grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantType) will overwrite the existing mapping, breaking the reverse lookup for previously issued tokens. While ConcurrentHashMap is used, the issue is logical - there's no uniqueness validation when dynamically adding grants, unlike the startup validation.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims there are 'two getters' returning conflicting grant values, but examining the diff shows only one getGrantType() method in the Context class (lines 169-172). The setFormParams method exists but there's no evidence it's intended for changing the grant type mid-flow - it's a setter for form parameters. The grantType is intentionally cached at construction time from the original form parameters. The finding misreads the code - there's no second getter for grant type, and the caching behavior appears intentional for preserving the original grant context throughout token processing.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/test/java/org/keycloak/protocol/oidc/encode/DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderTest.java:49 — The new tests construct the encoder without a session and only decode hand-authored IDs, leaving actual online/offline/transient session classification and client-versus-session lightweight settings unverified for consumers relying on the new context metadata (confidence 100; severity P2; advisory; code: `provider = new DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider(null, factory);`; rebuttal: the updated integration event matcher checks issuance, but it never asserts the session or token-type bytes, so it does not close this requirements-coverage gap).

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the new unit test (DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderTest) constructs the provider with a null session and only tests decoding of hand-crafted token IDs. Looking at the diff, the test does verify encode/decode round-trips for various scenarios (client credentials, offline, unknown grant type, old tokens), but it doesn't test getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext() which requires a real session to determine session type (online/offline/transient) and token type (lightweight/regular). The integration test matcher (isAccessTokenId) only checks the grant shortcut position, not the session-type or token-type bytes. This is a legitimate test coverage gap for the new functionality - the session classification logic in getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext() that checks userSession.getPersistenceState() and userSession.isOffline() is not covered by any test in this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: testsuite/integration-arquillian/tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/testsuite/AssertEvents.java:483 — The new event matcher accepts `onrtna:123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000` when authorization-code grant `ac` is expected because it reads positions 3–4 instead of 4–5 and rejects equality instead of inequality, so missing or incorrect grant propagation passes the authorization-code, refresh, device, and CIBA integration assertions (confidence 100; severity P2; blocking; code: `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`).

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies two bugs in the isAccessTokenId matcher at line 483: (1) substring(3, 5) reads characters at indices 3-4, but the grant shortcut is at positions 4-5 (indices 4 and 5), and (2) the condition uses .equals() with return false, meaning it returns false when the grant MATCHES (should be !equals or != to reject non-matches). This inverted logic means the matcher will incorrectly pass when grants don't match and fail when they do match.
